title: Does Alcohol Dehydrate You? How It Works and Signs to Watch
excerpt: Yes, alcohol dehydrates you by switching off the hormone that saves water. How much fluid you lose, which drinks are worst, the signs of dehydration, and how much it really explains your hangover.
metaDescription: Does alcohol dehydrate you? How alcohol blocks your water-saving hormone, which drinks dehydrate most, signs of dehydration, and how to rehydrate.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, alcohol does dehydrate you, but less dramatically than most people think. Alcohol switches off a hormone that normally tells your kidneys to hold on to water, so you pee more than you drank for a while. That fluid loss is real, and it explains your thirst, dry mouth, and dark morning urine. What it doesn't explain is the whole hangover. Research on hangovers suggests dehydration is one piece of the picture, alongside poor sleep, inflammation, low blood sugar, and the by-products of breaking down alcohol. So drinking water helps you feel less parched and less dizzy, but it won't make a heavy night disappear.

**The quick rules:** Have a glass of water with each alcoholic drink, and another before bed. Eat a real meal before you start. Stronger drinks (spirits, wine, shots) dehydrate you more per serving than beer does. If you were sweating, dancing, out in the heat, vomiting, or have diarrhea, you're losing much more fluid than alcohol alone would cause, and an electrolyte drink makes more sense than plain water. If you can't keep fluids down, feel faint when you stand, or stop peeing, get medical help.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research on alcohol and hydration. It isn't a substitute for a doctor who knows your health. **See a doctor or urgent care if** you can't keep any fluids down for more than a few hours, you vomit repeatedly, you haven't urinated in 8 hours or more, you feel faint or pass out when you stand, your heart keeps racing while you're resting, or you're confused. **Call 911 (or your local emergency number) right away** if someone who has been drinking can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, has a seizure, has blue-tinged or very pale cold skin, or is vomiting while barely conscious. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, not dehydration, and they need emergency care now. People with kidney disease, heart failure, diabetes, or who take diuretic ("water pill") medicines should ask their doctor how alcohol and fluid loss affect them.

## Does Alcohol Dehydrate You? The Short Science

Yes. Alcohol is a diuretic, meaning it makes you produce more urine. The key player is a hormone called **vasopressin**, also known as **antidiuretic hormone (ADH)**. Your brain releases vasopressin from the pituitary gland whenever your body needs to conserve water. Vasopressin travels to your kidneys and tells them to pull water back into your bloodstream instead of sending it to your bladder.

Alcohol blunts the release of vasopressin. With less of that "save the water" signal, your kidneys let more water pass straight through. You end up making more dilute, pale urine than you normally would, and more of it than the drink itself contained, at least while your blood alcohol level is climbing.

That's the whole reason you "break the seal" at the bar. It isn't that the first trip to the bathroom opens some valve. It's that alcohol has turned down your water-saving hormone, and your kidneys respond by sending water out steadily. If you want the full story of why the bathroom trips start and keep coming, our guide to [why alcohol makes you pee](/never-hungover/why-does-alcohol-make-you-pee) covers it in detail.

### Three things that change how much it dehydrates you

1. **How strong the drink is.** Research on this has found that stronger drinks cause a larger net fluid loss than weaker ones. A study by Hobson and Maughan (2010) found that a small dose of alcohol in stronger beer increased urine output compared with a weaker beer, while a later study of older men by Polhuis and colleagues (2017) found that wine and spirits caused a short-lived diuretic effect but beer did not. The simple reason is that beer brings a lot of water along with its alcohol, so the extra urine is partly or fully balanced by what you drank. A shot of vodka brings almost none.
2. **How hydrated you were to start with.** The same Hobson and Maughan study found that the diuretic effect was weaker in people who were already mildly dehydrated. Your body fights back when it's short on water. That's reassuring in one way, but it also means starting the night dehydrated (after a workout, a hot day, or a long flight) leaves you with less margin.
3. **Whether your blood alcohol is rising or falling.** The strongest water-losing effect happens while your blood alcohol level is going up. Once it plateaus and starts to drop, the effect fades. Studies have found that vasopressin levels can actually run higher than normal the morning after, as your body tries to correct the water deficit it built up overnight. In other words, the morning-after dry mouth is your body already working on the problem.

## How Much Water Does Alcohol Make You Lose?

You'll see precise-sounding numbers online, such as a specific number of milliliters of urine per gram of alcohol. Those figures trace back to small studies decades old, and real-world results vary a lot with the person, the drink, and what else they had. We'd rather not repeat a number as if it applied to everyone.

What's well supported is the pattern:

- **Spirits and shots:** the biggest net fluid loss per drink, because there's very little water in them.
- **Wine:** somewhere in between. A glass of wine is mostly water, but the alcohol content is high enough to push you into a net loss.
- **Beer:** the least dehydrating per serving, and in some studies close to neutral, because of the large volume of liquid. Higher-strength craft beers behave more like wine than light lager.
- **Cocktails with juice, soda, or ice:** the mixer adds water, which helps a bit. Caffeinated mixers (cola, energy drinks) add a mild extra diuretic push of their own, though regular caffeine users develop some tolerance to it.

For most people at a typical night out, the alcohol-driven fluid loss is noticeable but modest. The amount that actually leaves people badly dehydrated usually comes from the things that ride along with drinking: hours of dancing, hot crowded rooms, summer sun, a sauna or hot tub, vomiting, or diarrhea. Those can strip out far more water and salt than alcohol alone.

## Signs of Dehydration From Alcohol

Mild dehydration after drinking is common and usually fixes itself within a day once you drink fluids and eat. Here's what it tends to look like, from mild to more serious.

### Mild to moderate signs (common, usually manageable at home)

- **Thirst**, especially waking at 3 a.m. desperate for water
- **Dry mouth**, sticky saliva, or cracked lips
- **Dark yellow urine**, or peeing less often than usual the next morning
- **Headache**, often worse when you stand or move your head
- **Feeling tired, sluggish, or foggy**
- **Light-headedness when you stand up quickly**
- **Dry-feeling skin** or eyes

### More serious signs (take these seriously)

- Very dark urine, or **no urine for 8 hours or more**
- **Feeling faint or actually fainting** when you stand
- A **fast heartbeat that doesn't settle** when you sit or lie down
- **Being unable to keep fluids down** because of repeated vomiting
- **Confusion**, unusual irritability, or trouble staying awake
- **Muscle cramps** that keep coming back, which can point to low salt or potassium levels

If you're seeing the second list, plain sips of water at home may not be enough. Urgent care or an emergency room can give fluids through an IV, which is quick and effective when you truly can't keep anything down.

### Dehydration or alcohol poisoning?

These two can overlap, but they are not the same. Dehydration is a fluid problem. **Alcohol poisoning** is a dangerous level of alcohol in the blood that slows down the parts of your brain that control breathing, heart rate, and gag reflex. Someone who can't be woken, is breathing slowly or irregularly, is vomiting while passed out, has a seizure, or has cold, clammy, bluish skin needs **emergency care right now**. Don't let them "sleep it off," don't put them in a cold shower, and don't wait to see if it gets better. Call 911, keep them on their side, and stay with them.

> **When to see a doctor (for social drinkers):** Most next-morning thirst, headache, and dry mouth are normal and pass within a day. Get checked if you can't keep fluids down for more than a few hours, you haven't peed in 8 hours, you feel faint or your heart is racing at rest, symptoms are getting worse instead of better after 24 hours, or you have diabetes, kidney disease, heart disease, or take water pills. If someone is hard to wake, breathing oddly, or having a seizure, call 911.

## How Much of a Hangover Is Actually Dehydration?

This is where popular belief and research part ways. For decades, "dehydration" was the go-to explanation for hangovers. It's an easy story because the symptoms overlap: headache, thirst, fatigue, and dizziness are all signs of being low on fluid.

The research picture is more mixed. Reviews of hangover science, including work by the Alcohol Hangover Research Group, point to several factors working together:

- **Dehydration and fluid shifts**, which mainly drive thirst, dry mouth, and some of the headache and dizziness.
- **Poor sleep.** Alcohol helps you fall asleep but fragments the second half of the night, so you wake unrested. Our guide on [why you can't sleep after drinking](/never-hungover/cant-sleep-after-drinking) explains this.
- **Inflammation.** Heavy drinking raises markers of the immune system's inflammatory response, and that's been linked to how bad people feel.
- **Acetaldehyde.** When your liver breaks down alcohol, the first by-product is acetaldehyde, a toxic compound linked to nausea, flushing, and headache.
- **Low blood sugar.** Alcohol interferes with how your liver releases glucose, which can add to shakiness and weakness.
- **Congeners.** Darker drinks like bourbon and red wine contain more of these by-products of fermentation, and some studies have found they're linked to worse hangovers.

Two findings in particular suggest dehydration isn't the main driver. First, studies have found that blood markers of dehydration and electrolyte levels don't line up neatly with how severe people say their hangovers are. Second, survey research from the Alcohol Hangover Research Group found that people who drank water alongside alcohol still reported hangovers of similar severity overall, even though water helped with specific symptoms like thirst.

That doesn't mean hydration is useless. It means hydration is a real, helpful, partial fix. You'll likely feel less dried-out, less dizzy, and possibly less headachy. You won't fix the sleep loss, the inflammation, or the acetaldehyde with water alone. For a broader look at all the moving parts, see our breakdown of [hangover symptoms and what causes each one](/never-hungover/hangover-symptoms).

## Why You Wake Up So Thirsty After Drinking

The 3 a.m. thirst is one of the most recognizable effects of a night out. A few things combine to cause it:

1. **You spent the evening losing more water than you took in**, thanks to suppressed vasopressin and frequent bathroom trips.
2. **Alcohol can leave you breathing through your mouth while you sleep**, especially if you snore more after drinking, which dries your mouth further.
3. **Salty bar food and late-night snacks** raise the salt concentration in your blood, which triggers thirst on its own.
4. **As your blood alcohol falls, your body flips into water-saving mode**, and part of that is a strong drive to drink.

The fix is simple: keep a full glass or bottle of water by your bed before you go to sleep. You'll almost certainly reach for it.

## Does Alcohol Dehydrate Your Skin?

People often notice their skin looks dull, dry, or puffy after a night of drinking. Some of that is fluid-related, and some isn't.

- **Dryness:** net fluid loss can leave skin and lips feeling drier the next day. This usually resolves within a day or two once you're rehydrated.
- **Puffiness:** this sounds like the opposite of dehydration, but it's common. Alcohol widens blood vessels, salty food makes you retain water in the wrong places, and lying flat after drinking lets fluid pool in your face. Our guide to [alcohol face bloating](/never-hungover/alcohol-face-bloating) explains why it happens and how to bring it down.
- **Redness:** alcohol widens small blood vessels near the skin's surface, which is why some people look flushed.

Long-term, regular heavy drinking is associated with skin aging and conditions like rosacea flares, but one night out isn't going to change your skin in any lasting way.

## Hydration Strategy: Before, During, and After Drinking

Since you can't fully prevent alcohol's water-losing effect, the goal is to stay ahead of it. Here's a practical approach that doesn't require any special products.

### Before you drink

- **Start hydrated.** If your urine is pale yellow before you head out, you're in good shape. If it's dark, have a glass or two of water first.
- **Eat a real meal.** Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your blood, which flattens the steep rise that drives the strongest diuretic effect. Meals with protein, fat, fiber, and some salt are ideal.
- **Be extra careful after exercise, travel, or a hot day.** You're starting with less margin.

### While you drink

- **Alternate each alcoholic drink with a glass of water.** This is the most useful single habit. It replaces fluid as you go, and it also slows down how fast you drink, which lowers your peak blood alcohol.
- **Lean toward lower-strength drinks** if you're going to be out a long time. A light beer or a spritz with lots of soda water brings more water per unit of alcohol than straight spirits.
- **Watch the heat.** Dancing in a packed room or drinking in the sun at a festival or on a boat can multiply fluid loss. Sip water steadily, not just when you remember.
- **Skip the shots of hard liquor in a row.** That combination of fast drinking and almost no water is the most dehydrating pattern there is.

### Before bed

- **Drink one or two glasses of water.** You'll probably wake to pee, and that's fine. You'll also wake less parched.
- **Have a light snack with some salt** if you didn't eat much. Salt helps your body hold on to the water you just drank.
- **Put water by the bed** for the middle of the night.

### The morning after

- **Sip steadily rather than chugging.** A large volume all at once on an upset stomach can come straight back up. Small, frequent sips are better tolerated.
- **Eat something.** Food replaces salt and potassium, and many foods contain a lot of water. Fruit like watermelon and oranges, broth-based soups, and yogurt are all good options.
- **Check your urine.** When it's back to pale yellow, you're likely rehydrated.
- **Go easy on coffee.** Coffee is fine for most regular drinkers and the mild diuretic effect is largely offset by the water in the cup, but don't rely on it as your main fluid.

For a step-by-step morning-after plan, see our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking).

## Water vs. Electrolyte Drinks: What Actually Helps?

For a normal night of drinking where you didn't vomit or sweat heavily, **plain water and a meal are usually enough**. Alcohol's main effect is on water, not on salt, and food replaces the salt and potassium you lose.

Electrolyte drinks make more sense in specific situations:

- **You vomited or had diarrhea.** These strip out sodium and potassium along with water, and an oral rehydration drink (the kind designed for stomach bugs) replaces them better than water alone.
- **You were sweating a lot**, from dancing, heat, or exercise.
- **You feel light-headed when you stand**, which can be a sign your blood volume is low.
- **You can't face food yet.** An electrolyte drink can tide you over until you can eat.

What electrolyte drinks won't do is cure a hangover. They're a better tool for rehydrating, not a fix for the sleep loss, inflammation, and acetaldehyde that also make you feel awful. Sugar-heavy sports drinks also aren't ideal for rehydration if you're drinking a lot of them, since more sugar doesn't mean faster absorption. If you want to compare options, our guides on [whether water actually helps a hangover](/never-hungover/does-water-help-a-hangover), [when to take electrolytes around drinking](/never-hungover/electrolytes-before-or-after-drinking), and [electrolyte drinks for hangovers compared](/never-hungover/electrolyte-drinks-for-hangover-compared) go further. You can also make a simple version at home with water, a pinch of salt, a little sugar, and some citrus juice.

### What about IV drips?

Hangover IV clinics give a bag of fluid with electrolytes and sometimes vitamins or anti-nausea medicine. For someone who truly can't keep fluids down, IV fluids work quickly, which is exactly why ERs use them. For an ordinary hangover where you can drink normally, there's no good evidence that an IV drip does more than drinking fluids and eating would, and it costs much more.

## Who Is More Likely to Get Dehydrated From Alcohol?

Some people have less margin than others:

- **Older adults.** Thirst signals weaken with age, and the body holds less total water. The Polhuis study, which focused on older men, found a diuretic effect from wine and spirits in that group.
- **Smaller people and women on average**, who tend to have less total body water, so the same drink produces a higher blood alcohol level.
- **People on diuretics ("water pills")** for blood pressure or heart conditions, or on SGLT2 inhibitor diabetes medicines, which also increase urine output. Ask your doctor about alcohol if you take these.
- **People with diabetes**, since high blood sugar pulls water out through the kidneys, and alcohol can also make blood sugar swing in either direction.
- **People with kidney or heart disease**, for whom fluid balance matters more.
- **Anyone drinking in heat, at altitude, or after exercise.**
- **Anyone who also has a stomach bug** or is vomiting from drinking.

## Common Myths About Alcohol and Dehydration

**"Beer hydrates you."** Not really. Lower-strength beer is close to neutral for hydration in some studies, because its water content roughly balances the alcohol's effect. That's not the same as hydrating you. Water is still better.

**"If you drink enough water, you won't get a hangover."** There is no good evidence that drinking water prevents hangovers. It helps with dehydration symptoms like thirst and dizziness, but hangovers have several other causes.

**"Clear urine means you're fine to keep drinking."** Pale urine during a night of drinking often just means vasopressin is suppressed and your kidneys are flushing water. It's not a sign you're well hydrated or sober.

**"Coffee will dehydrate you further."** For regular coffee drinkers, the diuretic effect of a normal cup is small and mostly offset by the water in it. It's fine in moderation, though water should be your main fluid.

**"A hot shower, sauna, or hot tub will sweat it out."** No. You can't sweat out meaningful amounts of alcohol, and heat after drinking adds fluid loss and lowers blood pressure, which raises the risk of fainting. Skip the sauna until the alcohol has cleared.

## Where DHM Fits In

Hydration addresses one part of the morning after. Some people also use **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree, as part of their routine. DHM has interesting research on alcohol metabolism and on how alcohol affects GABA receptors in the brain, though much of it comes from animal studies, and human data is limited. There is no good evidence that DHM prevents dehydration, and it doesn't replace drinking water, eating, or pacing yourself.

If you'd like to try it alongside good hydration habits, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and the budget-friendly [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) explains how people typically use it, and our [guide to preventing hangovers](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) puts all the evidence-based habits in one place. As with any supplement, check with your doctor or pharmacist first if you take prescription medicines.

## The Bottom Line

Alcohol does dehydrate you, mainly by suppressing vasopressin, the hormone that tells your kidneys to keep water. Stronger drinks dehydrate you more than beer, and the effect is strongest while your blood alcohol is rising. That fluid loss explains the thirst, dry mouth, dark urine, and some of the headache and dizziness the next day. It doesn't explain the whole hangover, which also comes from poor sleep, inflammation, and alcohol's by-products. Alternate drinks with water, eat before and during, drink a glass or two before bed, and use an electrolyte drink if you were sweating or sick. And if someone can't keep fluids down, stops peeing, faints, or is hard to wake, get medical help rather than waiting it out.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does alcohol dehydrate you?**

Yes. Alcohol suppresses vasopressin (antidiuretic hormone), the hormone that tells your kidneys to hold on to water. With less of it, you pee out more fluid than usual while your blood alcohol is rising. Stronger drinks like spirits and wine cause more net fluid loss than beer, which brings a lot of water with it.

**What are the signs of dehydration from alcohol?**

Common signs are thirst, dry mouth, dark yellow urine, headache, fatigue, and light-headedness when you stand. More serious signs include no urine for 8 hours or more, fainting, a racing heart at rest, confusion, and being unable to keep fluids down. Those need medical attention, and someone who is hard to wake or breathing slowly needs emergency care for possible alcohol poisoning.

**Is a hangover just dehydration?**

No. Dehydration is one part of a hangover, mainly driving thirst, dry mouth, and some headache and dizziness. Research points to other major causes too, including poor sleep, inflammation, acetaldehyde (a toxic by-product of breaking down alcohol), low blood sugar, and congeners in darker drinks. That's why drinking water helps but doesn't fully prevent a hangover.

**Which alcohol dehydrates you the most?**

Spirits and shots cause the most net fluid loss per drink because they contain very little water. Wine is in the middle. Regular-strength or light beer is the least dehydrating per serving, and some studies found it close to neutral, because its water content offsets much of the alcohol's effect. Strong craft beers behave more like wine.

**How much water should I drink when drinking alcohol?**

A practical rule is one glass of water with each alcoholic drink, plus one or two glasses before bed. There's no exact formula that fits everyone, so use your urine color the next morning as a guide: pale yellow means you're likely rehydrated. Drink more if you're in the heat, dancing, or sweating.

**Are electrolyte drinks better than water after drinking?**

For an ordinary night out, water plus a meal is usually enough, since food replaces the salt and potassium you lose. Electrolyte or oral rehydration drinks make more sense if you vomited, had diarrhea, sweated heavily, or feel light-headed when you stand. They rehydrate you better in those cases, but they don't cure a hangover.

**How long does it take to rehydrate after drinking?**

For mild dehydration, most people feel noticeably better within a few hours of steadily sipping fluids and eating, and fully back to normal within about a day. If you still can't keep fluids down after several hours, haven't peed in 8 hours, or feel faint, see a doctor or urgent care, where IV fluids can help quickly.

**Does DHM prevent dehydration from alcohol?**

There is no good evidence that DHM prevents dehydration. DHM has research on alcohol metabolism and brain effects, mostly in animals with limited human data. It doesn't replace drinking water, eating, and pacing yourself, which remain the most reliable ways to limit fluid loss when you drink.
